title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
2. Competing regression models
Research question: How are handling of complaints, oppotunities to learn, and raises associated with overall workplace rating?
I expect all three predictors to be positively associated with the overall rating of the supervisor. First, the handling of complaints may be a strong predictor of the rating because employees may feel valued when their concerns are heard and addressed. Second, I expect learning opportunities and raises to be weaker predictors once complaints are accounted for. All three variables reflect how employees perceive their supervisor’s treatment of them, so they likely share considerable overlap. A supervisor who handles complaints fairly may also be seen as fair in offering learning opportunities and deciding raises. Thus, once complaints are controlled for, learning and raises may explain little additional variance in the rating.

Explore the fitted model
The meaning of the complaints coefficient changes as predictors are added. In M1, the coefficient (b = 0.75, SE = 0.10, p < .001) reflects the total association between complaints and rating: a 1-point increase in favourable complaint handling predicts a 0.75-point increase in rating. In M2, the coefficient decreases to 0.64 (SE = 0.12, p < .001) and reflects the unique association of complaints with rating when learning is controlled for. M3, the coefficient is similar (b = 0.65, SE = 0.14, p < .001) and represents the association when both learning and raises are held constant. Thus, complaints remains a strong and significant predictor in all three models, and its effect is largely independent of learning and raises.


Code
# Intercept-only model
mod0 <- lm(rating ~ 1, data = dat)

# Complaints model
mod1 <- lm(rating ~ complaints, data = dat)

# Complaints + learning model
mod2 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning, data = dat)

# Complaints+ learning + raises model
mod3 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning + raises, data = dat)

complaints_table <- bind_rows(
  tidy(mod1, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(Model = "M1: Complaints"),
  tidy(mod2, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(Model = "M2: + Learning"),
  tidy(mod3, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(Model = "M3: + Raises")
) |>
  filter(term == "complaints") |>
  mutate(Held.constant = c("None", "Learning", "Learning, raises")) |>
  select(Model, Held.constant, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

complaints_table |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Complaints Coefficient Across Models") |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    Held.constant = "Held constant",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    std.error = "SE",
    conf.low = "95% CI lower",
    conf.high = "95% CI upper",

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
3. Compare model performance


Code
#nested model comparisons
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

#select and rename
tests <- tests |>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) |>
  rename(
    Residual.df = Res.Df,
    Nested.Df = Df,
    Nested.F.stat = F,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>F)`
  )

#extract overall model performance
glance0 <- glance(mod0)
glance1 <- glance(mod1)
glance2 <- glance(mod2)
glance3 <- glance(mod3)

mods <- c(
  "M0: Null",
  "M1: Complaints",
  "M2: + Learning",
  "M3: + Raises"
)

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3
)

#Combine nested tests and model performance
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests
)

comparison_table <- comparison_table |>
  mutate(
    Delta.R2 = r.squared - lag(r.squared),
    
    RMSE = c(
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod0)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod1)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod2)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod3)^2))
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Model,
    r.squared,
    Delta.R2,
    adj.r.squared,
    RMSE,
    Residual.df,
    Nested.Df,
    Nested.F.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  )


#Display the combined model-comparison table
comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
    tab_header(title = "Comparison of Nested Regression Models Predicting Rating") |>
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Overall fit",
    columns = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, RMSE, Residual.df)
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Change from previous model",
    columns = c(Delta.R2, Nested.Df, Nested.F.stat, Nested.p.value)
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    r.squared = "R²",
    Delta.R2 = "ΔR²",
    adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²",
    RMSE = "RMSE",
    Residual.df = "Residual df",
    Nested.Df = "Nested df",
    Nested.F.stat = "Nested F",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      r.squared,
      Delta.R2,
      adj.r.squared,
      RMSE,
      Nested.F.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Delta.R2, Nested.Df, Nested.F.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )

Code
cmp <- comparison_table |>
  mutate(
    r2   = f3(r.squared),
    adj  = f3(adj.r.squared),
    rmse = f2(RMSE),
    dr2  = fp(Delta.R2),
    pct  = round(Delta.R2 * 100, 1),
    F    = f2(Nested.F.stat),
    p    = fp(Nested.p.value)
  )

m0 <- cmp[1, ]
m1 <- cmp[2, ]
m2 <- cmp[3, ]
m3 <- cmp[4, ]

df_den        <- min(comparison_table$Residual.df)
rmse_drop     <- -diff(comparison_table$RMSE)
rmse_drop_txt <- ifelse(rmse_drop < .01, "less than 0.01", f2(rmse_drop))
rmse_pct      <- round(rmse_drop[1] / comparison_table$RMSE[1] * 100)
sd_rating     <- f2(sd(dat$rating))


Both M2 and M3 explain the largest proportion of variation in rating (R² = .708), yet the pattern of results indicates that complaints carries almost all of the explanatory power. M1 alone accounts for 68.1% of the variance in rating, and this improvement over the null model is statistically significant, F(1, 26) = 60.73, p < .001. The addition of learning in M2 explains only 2.7% more variance, and this improvement is not significant, F(1, 26) = 2.38, p = .135. The addition of raises in M3 explains almost no additional variance (ΔR² < .001), F(1, 26) = 0.02, p = .876.
Adjusted R², which penalizes a model for each extra predictor, shows the same pattern. It rises slightly from .670 in M1 to .686 in M2 but then drops to .675 in M3, so raises costs a degree of freedom without any gain in fit.
RMSE, a measure of the average size of prediction errors, falls from 11.97 in M0 to 6.76 in M1. This reduction of about 5.21 points, or 44%, is clearly meaningful on a scale with an SD of 12.17. In contrast, learning lowers RMSE by only 0.29 points, and raises lowers it by less than 0.01 points, so neither change is substantively meaningful.

4. Evaluate regression diagnostics


Code
#selecting a provisional model
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = adj.r.squared,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

selected_name <- selected_row$Model

selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "M0: Null" = mod0,
  "M1: Complaints" = mod1,
  "M2: + Learning" = mod2,
  "M3: + Raises" = mod3
)

#Examine the assumptions/ regression diagnoatics
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(selected_model)









Code
#  multicollinearity 
vif_results <- check_collinearity(selected_model)
vif_results

Based on the largest adjusted R², the provisional model selection is M2: + Learning. The diagnostic plots suggest that this model meets its assumptions well enough to support the main conclusion about complaints.
First, the linearity assumption appears reasonable. In the Residuals vs Fitted plot, the red line stays flat around zero and shows no curved pattern. Second, the residuals look approximately normal, as most points in the Q–Q plot fall close to the diagonal. Third, no single department dominates the model. In the Residuals vs Leverage plot, every case falls inside the Cook’s distance contour of 0.5. Department 24 has the highest leverage, but its residual is small, so it pulls the fitted line very little. Fourth, multicollinearity does not appear to be a problem, as the largest VIF is 1.55.
A potential problem is uneven residual spread, as indicated in the Scale-Location plot. The red line drops near the middle of the range. This pattern suggests that predictions for departments with low ratings carry more error, so they should be interpreted with more caution.

I selected M2: + Learning as the preferred model. First, it has the highest adjusted R² (.686), compared with .670 for M1 and .675 for M3. Learning therefore adds slightly more explained variance than the penalty for one extra predictor. Second, M3 is not preferred because raises explains almost no additional variance and lowers adjusted R². Third, the diagnostic plots showed no serious violations, and two predictors keep the model simple and easy to interpret. However, the nested F-test showed that learning did not significantly improve fit beyond complaints (ΔR² = .027, p = .135). Thus, this model is a reasonable choice, but the contribution of learning should be interpreted with caution.


Code
coef_text <- coefficient_results |>
  mutate(
    across(c(estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high), f2),
    p = fp(p.value)
  )

comp  <- coef_text |> filter(term == "complaints")
learn <- coef_text |> filter(term == "learning")

sel <- cmp |> filter(Model == selected_name)


Complaint handling was positively associated with overall rating. Holding learning constant, a 1-point increase in the complaint handling predicted a 0.64-point increase in rating, 95% CI [0.40, 0.89], p < .001. The interval excludes zero, so this association is estimated with reasonable precision. Learning opportunities were also positively associated with rating. Holding complaint handling constant, a 1-point increase in learning predicted a 0.21-point increase in rating, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.49], p = .128. This interval includes zero, so the data are consistent with no unique association between learning and rating.
The selected model explained 70.8% of the variance in overall workplace ratings (R² = .708, adjusted R² = .686). Its RMSE was 6.47, so predicted ratings typically differed from observed ratings by about 6.5 points. This error is about half the SD of rating (12.17), but it is only slightly smaller than the RMSE of M1 (6.76).

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
6. Discussion and limitations
The results suggest that complaint handling is by far the most important of the three predictors for overall workplace ratings. First, complaints alone explained 68.1% of the variance in rating, and it remained a strong predictor after learning was held constant (b = 0.64, 95% CI [0.40, 0.89]). Second, learning opportunities added only 2.7% of explained variance, and this gain was not statistically significant (p = .135). Third, pay increases added almost no explained variance once complaints and learning were in the model (ΔR² < .001, p = .876). This pattern is consistent with my prediction that learning and raises overlap with complaint handling, as all three variables may reflect how fairly employees feel they are treated. Thus, for managers who want to improve how their departments are rated, the handling of employee complaints appears to be the most promising area to address.
These conclusions should be interpreted with several limitations in mind. First, the sample includes only 30 departments, so the estimates are imprecise, and the small sample offers limited power to detect modest effects such as that of learning. Second, the Scale-Location plot suggested that residual spread may not be constant, so predictions for low-rated departments are less precise.
